item.title: America's women's basketball epic reaches its climax with national unity on the line in FIBA World Cup final
item.description: Caitlin Clark and Angel Reese face France in the FIBA Women's World Cup final in Berlin as Team USA defends its 35-game winning streak Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
It's the final countdown.

Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and the U.S. women's national basketball team will defend its dynasty in Berlin on Sunday in a World Cup championship against France.

But this weekend, the pursuit of gold carries a distinctly heavier, and distinctly American, weight.

Taking the court on the 25th anniversary weekend of the September 11 terrorist attacks, head coach Kara Lawson isn't just looking to protect a historic 35-game World Cup winning streak.

"And as far as unity, I think unity is not just exclusive to the women’s basketball community," Lawson said. "I think it’s unity for our country as well. I think our team hopefully is creating unity across our country. People being proud about how we play and how we represent the red, white and blue."

TEAM USA COACH KARA LAWSON SPEAKS OUT ON PROGNOSTICATORS AFTER DOMINANT FIBA WORLD CUP WIN OVER HUNGARY

The French stand in the way of that hope.

France enters Sunday's championship undefeated. They just dismantled host-nation Germany 86-64 in the semifinals and jumped the U.S. for the top spot in FIBA’s power rankings heading into the final stage.

The French are also out for revenge.

Sunday marks a direct rematch of the unforgettable 2024 Olympic gold-medal thriller—a game the Americans narrowly escaped 67-66 only because French star Gabby Williams' toe grazed the 3-point line as time expired.

CAITLIN CLARK, ANGEL REESE SHOW UNITY FOR TEAM USA AT WORLD CUP AMID TENSE HISTORY

American women's basketball fans have been captivated by the surreal imagery of watching Clark and Reese play together as teammates in this World Cup.

In the team’s dominant 108-56 quarterfinal blowout against Hungary, the pair checked in together and completely overwhelmed the Hungarian defense, combining for 19 points and highlighting their growing on-court connection.

They've come together after three years as the sport's biggest rivals, with legions of fans that are often at each other's throats on social media. But now, the duo and their fans are on the same side, supporting America.

"We’ve played against each other so many times, so I’m sure we know each other’s game like the back of each other’s hand," Reese told TNT Sports on Thursday after a win over Hungary. "She dishes it off to me, I got one to her today, so, it’s fun. We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while."

Clark told The Associated Press before the quarterfinals, "We're both fiery, fiery competitors and we want to win and it's one of the things I really admire about [Reese's] game. She's competitive and she has a tremendous motor, like she has one of the best motors in the league. She works just as hard as anybody on the court."

Their emotional investment has been on display in a pair of clips captured by X user Michal Caro.

During their blowout win over Hungary, Reese and Clark were seen chatting and laughing while sitting on the bench.

Then, during a tense dogfight against Spain in the semifinal, the duo was seen sharing frustration and concerned expressions on the bench.

Clark and Reese highlight the group nicknamed the "young and turnt" crew, which has become a fan favorite term for Americans this World Cup. The nickname originated from fellow young teammate Paige Bueckers, who coined the term during a USA Basketball training camp in December 2025.

But their youth also earned them a spot outside of the team's starting lineup, as Reese, Clark and Bueckers, have all come off the bench in the U.S.'s five games so far. Lawson has remained committed to starting the veterans for the U.S.'s World Cup run, sparking debate among fans among social media.

However, Lawson has also suggested she would be open to adjusting the lineup.

"I think that our starting group's done a pretty good job of getting us off to good starts, and rotationally from game to game we could change things, but I like where we are right now," Lawson said Wednesday before the quarterfinal.

France's key players view Team USA as summer teammates, workout partners and daily WNBA rivals.

Marine Johannès, a New York Liberty player, has spent years sharing a locker room and playing alongside Team USA veteran leader and Liberty teammate Breanna Stewart.

Johannès was ready and expecting to take on the U.S. in the championship before the Americans had even punched their ticket to the final.

"If I'm honest, we have nothing to lose. We actually know they're a great team. They won every World Cup for years and years. They are really talented. We all know that. We are playing with these players all season in the W, we know how good they are," Johannès told reporters after her team defeated Germany in the semifinal, hours before the U.S. took the court against Spain. "It's one game. Nothing to lose. We are going to play hard, and we'll see what happens."

France's star, Williams enters Sunday's final playing some of the most dominant basketball of her career. In the semifinals, Williams helped orchestrate France’s commanding 86-64 blowout of host-nation Germany, completely silencing a raucous, high-energy home crowd in Berlin.

"I've been through quite a few moments like that. I know what that kind of pressure is like," Williams said. "I know what's needed in those moments."

Born in Nevada, Williams came up through America's premier women's basketball institution, UConn, where she won two national championships and shared the floor for years with current U.S. star Napheesa Collier.

Her time in the WNBA has given her hands-on experience defending and scoring against virtually every player on the American roster. For Williams, facing Team USA isn't a showdown against an unfamiliar juggernaut, but an opportunity to settle a score with players she has grown up alongside after Olympic heartbreak in 2024.

For all the tactical matchups on the court, Sunday's championship carries a distinctly heavier cultural weight in a highly polarized calendar year for women’s basketball—and for the United States in a heated midterm year.

The WNBA season that preceded this World Cup break was defined by tribalism. Phoenix Mercury star Alyssa Thomas punched Clark in the throat, prompting a suspension and overwhelming backlash from Clark's large passionate fan base. Toronto Tempo coach Sandy Brondello was suspended after calling Reese a "protected species" igniting even more race-related discourse on social media.

Then came the Sophie Cunningham rallies and a national phenomenon over the incursion of the "Save Women's Sports" movement into the WNBA.

Tensions escalated when Chicago Sky player DiJonai Carrington was ejected for hitting Cunningham and subsequently sparked a racial controversy by posting about "white privilege" on social media.

The friction spilled directly into the stands when former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom, who was attending a game to publicly support Cunningham, was ejected from the arena following a heated courtside confrontation with Chicago guard Natasha Cloud.

And then it was announced that WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert would be retiring at the end of the year, signaling a need more change in the WNBA moving forward.

But now as the tournament has progressed, Americans who may have found themselves on opposite sides of the Clark-Reese debate are now jointly lobbying for the two stars to start together, and the intrigue has led to record-breaking TV ratings for the FIBA World Cup.

According to TNT Sports U.S., the USA-Italy game averaged 1.3 million viewers and peaked at 1.7 million. The USA-Czechia game averaged 1.2 million viewers, peaking at 1.4 million, while the USA-China opener averaged 577,000 and peaked at 694,000.

And at the heart of Team USA's mission is unapologetic patriotism.

Stewart, who has been representing the country internationally since she was 14 years old, emphasized that setting aside rivalries to put on the American jersey remains the ultimate honor.

"It feels great. I think that any time I can represent Team USA I want to," Stewart said ahead of the knockout rounds. "I've had the incredible opportunity of being able to do it for a long time and since I was really young, and every time I get the call I want to show up."

OutKick can confirm that the entire Team USA roster has stood proudly for the national anthem ahead of the quarterfinal and semifinal games.

The timing of the final, taking place the same weekend as the 25th anniversary of 9/11, was felt by Lawson and her players.

Lawson noted that she heavily felt the somber weight of the moment all the way in Berlin, and hopes a gold-medal finish can offer a moment of healing for Americans back home.

"I think, you know, being a part of USA Basketball for so long, there’s a great pride in it," Lawson said. "I mean, from when I was 17 years old until now, being a part of it in different capacities, you know, I think—I don’t know if there’s anyone prouder to represent the U.S. than I am in this capacity.

"And so we think about that. And I felt the presence of the U.S. here, even though we are in Europe. I felt it, and certainly felt it yesterday in 9/11 and, you know, a somber anniversary."

When the ball tips off in Berlin against France, Team USA will be fighting to protect a 35-game World Cup winning streak and a multi-decade basketball empire. But more importantly, they will be playing for a divided nation tuning in back home, hoping to offer an undisputed moment of American greatness.

item.title: Jason Chaffetz: 4 ways to make football more exciting to watch
item.description: Former Rep. Jason Chaffetz argues the NFL kicking game has become too predictable and lays out four ways the league could make field goals, extra points and kickoffs more exciting.
item.content:encoded:
It’s time to "fix the kick" in the NFL.  

With the Chief’s Harrison Butker’s 69-yard field goal in the pre-season, it was demonstrated yet again that today’s kickers are better than ever.  Year after year they kick it higher, further, and straighter.  Usually, the placekicker is the leading scorer on the team, but nobody cares because the kicking game has become boring and predictable. The NFL failed to make it more interesting when they moved back extra points and changed kickoffs. Here are four ways to boot it up a big notch:

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Make it a rectangle that challenges the placekicker to "place" it in the uprights, without kicking it too high, where the referee has to make a judgment call about whether the kick was between the posts.  

This will make every kick more interesting. 38-yard kicks are too routine.  Extra points are so boring it’s time to go get a snack.

All NFL level kickers can hit 70–80-yard field goals in practice.  More and more coaches are taking chances that their guy can hit it from more than 50 yards out.

The primary difference between high school, college, and pro kicking is distance with trajectory.  Lining up approximately 7.5 yards behind the line of scrimmage, the defense surges so they are usually about 5 yards from the kick coming off the ground.  The pros need to get the ball at least 11 feet in the air to avoid it being blocked.  It’s hard to do, but they all do it with relative ease.  

Time to make it more difficult.  Let’s change the "field goal" to an actual goal.

Similar to golf, kickers use their 9-iron on all kicks.  They are only challenged to hit it long and straight.  Kicking it into the target is much different, more challenging, and will be more exciting to watch.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Who’s ready to watch the NFL’s fastest players race each other to start the game? Let’s line up one player from each team on the same goal line.  When the referee blows the whistle, the two players sprint to the game ball on the 50-yard line.  Whoever recovers the ball gets possession for his team, starting at their own 20-yard line.  Should neither team recover the ball in bounds, the home team will take possession at the 50-yard line.

The scoring team will have the ball at their own 35-yard line. They have one play to advance 20 yards and retain possession. If not, the defending team takes possession. Essentially, this replaces the on-side kick.

Most teams will opt to punt. The average NFL punt is 46.7 yards. Usually the ball will sail through the air and land roughly at the 20-yard line. Just like other live punts, the receiving team can block the kick, call for a fair catch or return it. Suddenly, there is a whole bunch of strategy at play. Because the teams line up on the line of scrimmage, the safety concerns of previous kickoffs aren’t a concern, but live punts are a lot more exciting than the current kickoff system.

A strong kicker on the team that gets first possession in overtime isn’t good for the game. Instead, use the same rules as the college football playoffs and most high schools. Each team gets a possession. No coin toss. The home team gets to make the decision about what to do on the first possession and, if tied, then they alternate. This continues in perpetuity until there is a winner.

With these four changes, games will become far less predictable, far more fun to watch, and will force teams to use more strategy, skill and speed.

The NFL should try all three pre-season games next year to see how it goes.

And while they are at it, here are two more suggestions: start using the bigger, softer, safer helmets and please stop the long halftime lip-syncing concerts. We just want to watch some football, starting with a sprint to midfield to fight for possession of the ball.

________

Jason Chaffetz was a placekicker at BYU and a former Member of Congress.  He is now a Fox News Contributor and host of the Jason in the House podcast.

item.title: AI robot for seniors can alert family after a call for help
item.description: Tuya Smart's Doova AI home robot rolls to seniors who call for help and connects family via live video, but key privacy questions remain unanswered.
item.content:encoded:
If you have a parent or grandparent who wants to stay in their own home, you probably know the question that can sit quietly in the back of your mind: What happens if they fall and nobody realizes they need help? Tuya Smart thinks its small artificial intelligence robot could become part of the answer.

The company unveiled Doova at IFA 2026 in Berlin. This wheeled AI home companion is designed for seniors who live independently. It can move through the home, respond when someone calls for help and connect family members through live video when an emergency appears to be unfolding.

That gets my attention because Doova goes beyond sitting on a table waiting for someone to press a button or call out from across the room. It can actually come to you. And that raises a bigger question: How much could a robot like this really help someone live safely and independently at home?

NEW! Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Health Care With AI

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you take a more active role in your health care. You’ll learn how to organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare questions for your next doctor’s visit. No technical experience is needed.

Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com

THE BEST TIME TO TALK TO YOUR PARENTS ABOUT SENIOR CARE — BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE

Doova uses LDS LiDAR to navigate around the home. A four-microphone system helps it figure out where a voice is coming from. Meanwhile, AI vision analyzes a person's skeletal posture.

If someone falls or needs assistance, they can say, "Hey Tuya, help." Doova then locates the person and rolls over to assess what is happening. Tuya says that if the user does not respond within 60 seconds, Doova starts an emergency response workflow. Family members receive an alert with a two-way live video call so they can see what is happening and arrange assistance.

For now, Tuya has not said that Doova automatically detects falls without the user first calling for help or that it directly contacts 911 or a professional monitoring service. So, I would treat it as an added layer of support rather than a replacement for a dedicated medical alert system.

Emergency help is only part of what Tuya has built into Doova. The robot uses a multimodal large language model so people can talk with it in a more natural way instead of memorizing rigid voice commands.

For someone spending long stretches at home alone, Doova can carry on a conversation or play entertainment. It can also help make sense of a confusing bill or letter. Another feature caught my eye. Tuya says Doova can identify potential scam risks.

YOUR SENIOR PARENTS ARE EASIER TO IMPERSONATE THAN YOU ARE

That could be useful for older adults who receive a suspicious message and want a second opinion before responding. However, I would never want someone relying solely on an AI robot to decide whether a bill, email or financial request is legitimate.

AI can make mistakes. If Doova flags something suspicious, the safest next move would still be to verify it independently or share it with someone you trust. We've seen how much personal information scammers can gather about older adults, particularly after major life changes such as moving into a retirement community.

A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME

Doova can remind you to take medication, keep track of your schedule and give you weather updates. Tuya says it can also learn your preferences over time, which could make its suggestions feel more useful day-to-day.

The company plans to add a feature that helps find misplaced items around the house. If that works well, I can see the appeal. Plenty of us have spent far too long looking for glasses, keys or a remote that was nearby the whole time.

WOULD YOU PAY $8,000 FOR A ROBOT TO FOLD LAUNDRY?

Doova also doubles as a mobile home-monitoring device. Rather than continuously hugging the walls as some patrol robots do, Tuya says Doova travels to selected locations near the center of rooms. From there, it can perform a 360-degree scan.

The robot then creates a safety report that can be sent to the user's phone. When the battery runs low, Doova can return to its charging dock on its own.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

That gives the robot another possible use when someone travels or spends part of the day away from home. However, this capability also leads straight into the biggest question I have about Doova.

Doova has microphones, AI vision and live video inside the home. It can also learn a user's preferences over time. That can make the robot more helpful, but it also means giving it access to a lot of personal information.

We raised similar questions when we looked at another AI home robot that can recognize family members and build personalized memories. With Doova, I would want to know where video and audio are processed, what gets stored, who can see it and whether users can permanently delete what the robot has learned.

Tuya's launch announcement does not spell out those Doova-specific privacy controls. Until it does, that is something I would look closely at before bringing a camera-equipped AI robot into a loved one's home. You can also review our guide to limiting the information popular AI services collect about you.

Tuya also designed Doova to work as a central smart home controller. A senior could use voice commands to adjust connected lights or curtains. Doova can also interact with compatible kitchen and bathroom devices.

I like the thinking here. Smart homes can become complicated very quickly, especially when every device has its own app. If Doova can put those controls into a simple conversation, that could make smart home technology far easier to use.

The robot has a 10.1-inch HD display with animated facial expressions. Its rounded design also looks more like a friendly household companion than an industrial machine.

There are still some important blanks to fill in. Tuya has not announced a retail price or when consumers will actually be able to buy Doova. I also want to see how it handles a real home. Rugs, cords and tight spaces can trip up mobile robots. Stairs are another obvious challenge for something that moves around on wheels.

The bigger question is how dependable Doova would be during an actual emergency. Someone may be frightened, speaking softly or lying somewhere the robot cannot easily reach. That is where real-world testing will tell us much more than a demonstration on the show floor.

We reached out to Tuya Smart with questions about Doova's emergency response, privacy protections, connectivity and availability, but did not hear back before our deadline.

If you are helping a parent or loved one age in place, Doova gives us a pretty good look at where home technology is heading. Instead of relying only on stationary smart speakers or cameras, future AI assistants may move around the house and respond to what is happening nearby.

That could give families another way to stay connected while allowing older adults to maintain more independence. However, I would look closely at the emergency process before relying on any product like this. Find out who gets contacted and what happens when the internet fails. You should also understand exactly what the cameras and microphones collect.

Finally, think about the person who will actually use it. The best technology in the world offers little value if someone finds it confusing, intrusive or uncomfortable.

What interests me most about Doova is the move from passive smart devices toward AI that can physically come to you. For an older adult who wants to remain independent, having a robot respond to a call for help and bring family into the situation quickly could offer real peace of mind.

Still, I would want much more information before trusting Doova with someone I love. Safety technology has to prove itself outside the controlled environment of a trade show. I want to know how reliably it reaches someone during an emergency and how much personal information it collects along the way.

The privacy side deserves just as much attention. A moving camera and microphone that learns your routines can become incredibly helpful. It can also become one of the most intimate connected devices in your home. Doova has an interesting idea at its core. Now Tuya needs to show that the technology can earn the level of trust its role requires.

Would you put an AI robot with cameras and microphones in an aging parent's home if it could help family respond faster during an emergency, or would that feel like too much surveillance? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.
